extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-form philosophical exposition (metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics) that articulates the nature and method of philosophy, the role of art and music, and the metaphysical status of life, death, and the present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's proper aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy can never do more than interpret and explain what is given; it should retain a purely contemplative attitude and investigate, not prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect moral precepts or doctrine of duty from philosophy; it should not attempt to 'guide conduct' or 'transform character.' Philosophy brings distinct abstract knowledge of the nature of the world but is not a practical recipe for producing virtue or genius. (Text: "Philosophy can never do more than interpret and explain what is given... it should retain a purely contemplative attitude, and should investigate, not prescribe.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of genuine philosophical consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The genuine philosophical method 'does not concern itself with the whence, the whither, and the why of the world, but always and everywhere demands only the what.' It abstracts from the forms of the principle of sufficient reason to reach the inner nature of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'historical philosophising' (cosmogonies, doctrines of successive emanations, or doctrines of constant becoming) and any appeal to temporal 'becoming'; instead seek that which remains when forms of relation are abstracted — the inner nature (Ideas) of the world. (Text: "The method which considers things not according to any relation... but, on the contrary, just that which remains when all that belongs to the form of knowledge proper to that principle has been abstracted, the inner nature of the world.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should not posit an 'absolute ought' or law of freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not expect an 'absolute ought' or an universal law of freedom from philosophical investigation; such notions contain contradictions and are inadequate for mature philosophical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book will not speak of 'ought' as a universal prescription; calling the will free and prescribing laws for it is contradictory. Moral systems and abstract concepts are unfruitful for producing virtue—virtue cannot be taught. (Text: "The dead conceptions of philosophy do not decide the matter... We shall not speak at all of 'ought'...")

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's function: render the world-as-idea more distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of art is to render the visibility of the world-as-idea more distinct; art is the 'camera obscura' that shows objects more purely and enables clearer comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art achieves what the visible world itself does but with greater concentration, intention and intelligence, and thus is 'the flower of life.' The artist contemplates the objectification of will and copies it, gaining consolation though not permanent deliverance. (Text: "If the whole visible world is just the objectification, the mirror, of the will... the work of art is to render this visibility more distinct. It is the camera obscura which shows the objects more purely.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's nature and limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is perceived in and through time alone, with absolute exclusion of space, and apart from the influence of causality; it makes the aesthetic impression as effect without obliging us to go back to causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfectly accurate system of music is 'arithmetically impossible' (intonation tensions among intervals), so all possible music deviates from perfect purity and must 'conceal the discords' by temperament. Music's perception is temporal and non-causal, giving it a distinct aesthetic role. (Text: "I might still have something to say about the way in which music is perceived, namely, in and through time alone... A complete, pure, harmonious system of tones is not only physically but arithmetically impossible.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical investigation as descriptive, not prescriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering human action (ethics) philosophically, the task is to exhibit and explain the action of men in its inner nature and content, not to provide prescriptive maxims or 'universal receipts' for virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat human action as the expression of the will and reason's capacity to survey the whole; present ethical theory as an interpretation grounded on prior metaphysical claims, not as a set of practical commands. (Text: "Our philosophy will maintain the same immanency in the case of action... endeavour to exhibit... action of men in its inner nature and content.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Present as the essential form of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the phenomenon of will (life, reality) is really only the present; past and future exist only as conception within knowledge, so the present alone is the form of all life and its sure possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical consequences: fear of death as loss of the present is an illusion; suicide is vain because life (the will) is assured and the present endures. Use analogies (rock in a stream, tangent to a revolving sphere) to illustrate the primacy of the present. (Text: "Above all things, we must distinctly recognise that the form of the phenomenon of will... is really only the present...")

rubrics_metrics.name: Value belongs to Ideas/species, not to individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature cares for the species rather than the individual; individuals are ephemeral phenomena whose permanence is not the concern of Nature; only Ideas (the species, the objective forms) possess true reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains cultural practices (feasts on sarcophagi, Siva with lingam) that point the mourner from individual death to the immortal life of Nature; philosophically, one should accept individuation as transient and focus on the Idea. (Text: "It is not the individual, but only the species that Nature cares for... Therefore she is always ready to let the individual fall.")

rubrics_metrics.name: On death and the will: death affects the phenomenon, not the thing-in-itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth and death belong to the phenomenon (life) as conditions of individuation; they do not affect the will as thing-in-itself nor the pure subject of knowing, which lie outside time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this view, the individual’s fear of annihilation is grounded in confusion between phenomenon and thing-in-itself; philosophical knowledge can mitigate fear by placing the individual in the perspective of the whole. (Text: "That which constantly becomes and passes away... belongs to the phenomenon as such... but the will itself as thing-in-itself is not affected by it.")
